commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether mapping workflows and specifying users, insertion point, actor, and follow-on intervention improves how AI outputs are acted upon, although twelve sources endorse the practice. Two hazard studies suggest that undefined roles and missing response protocols are common in real deployments and may leave AI outputs unacted upon.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The two supplied studies are level 3 descriptive and pre-post designs that document the hazard. They show that a problem exists, but they cannot show that workflow mapping solves it. The twelve endorsements rest on expert consensus and commentary rather than comparative data.

In a survey of 97 stroke care providers, 37.5% reported formal protocol integration and 43.6% had designated personnel for AI alert response. An alert with no assigned responder is a failure mode in which a correct output never reaches the patient. Whether specifying the actor in advance closes this gap has not been measured.

Across nine English outpatient services, many staff struggled to act on model risk scores when the task fell outside their defined roles, and intervention call rates were low in phase 1 and lower in phase 2. This suggests that role definition may affect fidelity, though the study did not test a mapped workflow against an unmapped one.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions asks developers to understand the context of use and identify user tasks before designing transparency features. The NIST generative AI profile lists intended users among its considerations. Neither source makes workflow mapping a deployer obligation, and no study links either one to outcomes.

Neither hazard study reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One commentary endorsing the practice suggests that workflow diagrams may help identify sources of bias, but no supplied data test that claim in any population.

The English study found that intervention call volumes fell between phases when staff did not see the work as part of their roles. This suggests that adding AI-triggered tasks without assigned staffing may produce little activity. The cost and staff time needed to map workflows before deployment were not reported in either study.

When fewer than half of surveyed stroke providers had designated personnel for AI alerts, patients may be flagged by a system with no clear person responsible for following up. A written plan naming who acts on each output could support patients' ability to reach a human, but this benefit has not been studied.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments that used prespecified workflow maps, naming users, insertion point, responsible actor, and follow-on intervention, with deployments that did not. Useful designs would include stepped-wedge or controlled before-after studies that measure the share of AI outputs acted upon, time to action, clinician burden, and patient outcomes, along with the staff time and cost of the mapping itself.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice, and neither hazard study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether workflow mapping works for them or whether roles such as interpreter or community health worker need to be specified in the design.
